Development of scalable and generalizable mechanistic interpretability frameworks
Establishment of a unified theoretical framework for reasoning in LRMs
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has catalyzed the emergence of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) that have pushed reasoning capabilities to new heights. While their performance has garnered significant excitement, exploring the internal mechanisms driving these behaviors has become an equally critical research frontier. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of the mechanistic understanding of LRMs, organizing recent findings into three core dimensions: 1) training dynamics, 2) reasoning mechanisms, and 3) unintended behaviors. By synthesizing these insights, we aim to bridge the gap between black-box performance and mechanistic transparency. Finally, we discuss under-explored challenges to outline a roadmap for future mechanistic studies, including the need for applied interpretability, improved methodologies, and a unified theoretical framework.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Back Attention: Understanding and Enhancing Multi-Hop Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models perform latent multi-hop reasoning, and how can this ability be enhanced?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces back attention, a novel mechanism that allows lower layers to capture higher-layer hidden states, enhancing multi-hop reasoning in LLMs. Also introduces logit flow, an interpretability method for tracing logit propagation.
papers.conclusion: The analysis provides new insights into multi-hop reasoning mechanisms and introduces back attention, a powerful and lightweight method that significantly enhances reasoning accuracy in LLMs by allowing lower layers to access higher-layer features.
papers.key_findings:
Identifies four distinct stages in single-hop knowledge prediction: entity subject enrichment, entity attribute extraction, relation subject enrichment, and relation attribute extraction.
Finds that failures in multi-hop reasoning often stem from the relation attribute extraction stage, where conflicting logits reduce prediction accuracy.
Proposes back attention, which enables a 1-layer transformer to achieve the performance of a 2-layer transformer on arithmetic tasks.
Back attention, when fine-tuned on a single layer of pre-trained LLMs, significantly improves accuracy across five reasoning datasets and four different models.
Logit flow provides a neuron-level perspective on information flow, offering a more granular understanding than layer-level methods like activation patching.
papers.limitation:
The interpretability analysis primarily focuses on single-hop and two-hop knowledge queries, which represent specific reasoning scenarios; other reasoning tasks might involve different mechanisms.
Back attention is applied to only a single layer in this work, though it could be extended to two or more layers for potentially greater improvements.
future_direction: Extend back attention to two or more layers.
Validate the findings on more diverse reasoning tasks to refine the interpretability framework for broader applicability.
papers.abstract: We investigate how large language models perform latent multi-hop reasoning in prompts like "Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart's mother's spouse is". To analyze this process, we introduce logit flow, an interpretability method that traces how logits propagate across layers and positions toward the final prediction. Using logit flow, we identify four distinct stages in single-hop knowledge prediction: (A) entity subject enrichment, (B) entity attribute extraction, (C) relation subject enrichment, and (D) relation attribute extraction. Extending this analysis to multi-hop reasoning, we find that failures often stem from the relation attribute extraction stage, where conflicting logits reduce prediction accuracy. To address this, we propose back attention, a novel mechanism that enables lower layers to leverage higher-layer hidden states from different positions during attention computation. With back attention, a 1-layer transformer achieves the performance of a 2-layer transformer. Applied to four LLMs, back attention improves accuracy on five reasoning datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in enhancing latent multi-hop reasoning ability.

papers.title: Dissecting Long-Chain-of-Thought Reasoning Models: An Empirical Study
papers.research_question: What are the roles of positive and negative samples in scaling RL for long-chain-of-thought reasoning models? How can we address data inefficiency in GRPO? What causes unstable performance during evaluation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper empirically analyzes the training dynamics of long-chain-of-thought reasoning models, revealing that positive samples primarily aid fitting to training data while negative samples enhance generalization and robustness. It also addresses data inefficiency in GRPO and explains unstable evaluation performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper analyzes three key aspects of training and evaluating long-CoT reasoning models, providing insights that may aid in developing more robust, data-efficient, and stable reasoning models.
papers.key_findings:
Positive samples help the model fit the training data, while negative samples improve generalization and robustness.
In cold-start scenarios, training sequentially on negative then positive samples yields better generalization without sacrificing performance.
Positive samples are crucial for convergence in zero-RL training by enabling instruction following.
Data inefficiency in GRPO: over half of samples yield zero advantage and do not contribute to training.
Relative length reward (RLR) can encourage more efficient reasoning without sacrificing performance.
Unstable evaluation performance is caused by uncertain problems, and greedy decoding can distort evaluation by flipping response correctness.
papers.abstract: Despite recent progress in training long-chain-of-thought reasoning models via scaling reinforcement learning (RL), its underlying training dynamics remain poorly understood, and several counterintuitive behaviors persist. This work focuses on three key aspects: (1) We systematically analyze the roles of positive and negative samples in scaling RL, revealing that positive samples mainly facilitate precise fitting to the training data, whereas negative samples significantly enhance generalization and robustness. Interestingly, while positive samples are essential for convergence in the zero-RL setting, training on negative samples alone suffices to attain strong reasoning performance and even better generalization in cold-start scenarios. (2) We identify substantial data inefficiency in group relative policy optimization, where over half of the samples yield zero advantage. To address this, we explore two strategies, including relative length rewards and offline sample injection, to leverage these data better and enhance reasoning efficiency and capability. (3) We investigate unstable performance across various reasoning models and benchmarks, attributing instability to uncertain problems with ambiguous outcomes, and demonstrate that greedy decoding can distort evaluation by flipping the correctness of responses. Our code is available at: https://github.com/takagi97/Dissect-Long-Reason-Models.

papers.title: SelfIE: Self-Interpretation of Large Language Model Embeddings
papers.research_question: How can we interpret the hidden embeddings of large language models in natural language to reveal their internal reasoning and enable control over model behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SelfIE, a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own hidden embeddings in natural language, and extends it to control model behavior via supervised and reinforcement control on embeddings.
papers.conclusion: SelfIE provides a powerful framework for interpreting and controlling LLM reasoning by generating text descriptions of hidden embeddings, opening avenues for transparent and reliable model behavior.
papers.key_findings:
SelfIE can elicit implicit world state knowledge in embeddings without training, matching the performance of a 100-shot linear probe.
SelfIE reveals internal reasoning processes behind complex LLM behaviors such as harmful knowledge recall, prompt injection, ethical decisions, physics reasoning, social reasoning, and hallucination.
SelfIE-based supervised control can edit fact associations and open-ended concepts with good generalization, requiring gradient computation only for individual layers.
SelfIE-based reinforcement control can erase harmful knowledge in LLMs without supervised targets, reducing prompt injection success rate by 84.66%.
SelfIE-based control can override user-specified ethical preferences, increasing fairness in LLM responses with a 95% effective rate.
future_direction: Further exploration of reasoning patterns in LLMs and model reasoning behavior controls with hidden embeddings.
papers.abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) obtain their answers? The ability to explain and control an LLM's reasoning process is key for reliability, transparency, and future model developments. We propose SelfIE (Self-Interpretation of Embeddings), a framework that enables LLMs to interpret their own embeddings in natural language by leveraging their ability to respond to inquiries about a given passage. Capable of interpreting open-world concepts in the hidden embeddings, SelfIE reveals LLM internal reasoning in cases such as making ethical decisions, internalizing prompt injection, and recalling harmful knowledge. SelfIE's text descriptions on hidden embeddings also open up new avenues to control LLM reasoning. We propose Supervised Control, which allows editing open-ended concepts while only requiring gradient computation of individual layer. We extend RLHF to hidden embeddings and propose Reinforcement Control that erases harmful knowledge in LLM without supervision targets.

papers.title: A Survey on Latent Reasoning
papers.research_question: This paper investigates latent reasoning as an alternative to explicit chain-of-thought in large language models, exploring its methods, benefits, and future directions.
papers.core_contribution: This survey provides a comprehensive overview of latent reasoning, categorizing methods into activation-based and hidden state-based approaches, and discusses future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition.
papers.conclusion: The survey unifies perspectives on latent reasoning and charts future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition.
papers.key_findings:
Latent reasoning performs multi-step inference in continuous hidden states, offering higher bandwidth than explicit chain-of-thought.
Activation-based methods create deeper computational graphs by iteratively processing information through the same layers.
Hidden-state-based methods expand temporal capacity by evolving hidden states over sequences.
Diffusion models enable infinite-depth reasoning through bidirectional context and iterative refinement.
Layer specialization theory suggests different layers play distinct roles in latent reasoning, analogous to steps in explicit CoT.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities, especially when guided by explicit chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning that verbalizes intermediate steps. While CoT improves both interpretability and accuracy, its dependence on natural language reasoning limits the model's expressive bandwidth. Latent reasoning tackles this bottleneck by performing multi-step inference entirely in the model's continuous hidden state, eliminating token-level supervision. To advance latent reasoning research, this survey provides a comprehensive overview of the emerging field of latent reasoning. We begin by examining the foundational role of neural network layers as the computational substrate for reasoning, highlighting how hierarchical representations support complex transformations. Next, we explore diverse latent reasoning methodologies, including activation-based recurrence, hidden state propagation, and fine-tuning strategies that compress or internalize explicit reasoning traces. Finally, we discuss advanced paradigms such as infinite-depth latent reasoning via masked diffusion models, which enable globally consistent and reversible reasoning processes. By unifying these perspectives, we aim to clarify the conceptual landscape of latent reasoning and chart future directions for research at the frontier of LLM cognition. An associated GitHub repository collecting the latest papers and repos is available at: https://github.com/multimodal-art-projection/LatentCoT-Horizon/.

papers.title: MARCOS: Deep Thinking by Markov Chain of Continuous Thoughts
papers.research_question: How can we re-imagine reasoning in large language models to overcome the drawbacks of token-based chain-of-thought, such as slow inference, information bottleneck, and entangled thinking and speaking?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces MARCOS, a new paradigm that models reasoning as a Markov chain of continuous thoughts, decoupling thinking from speaking, which achieves performance comparable to or better than token-based chain-of-thought with significant inference speedup.
papers.conclusion: MARCOS presents a new paradigm for latent thinking in LLMs, achieving state-of-the-art reasoning performance and efficiency, while enabling step-level control over randomness and opening avenues for reinforcement learning and non-autoregressive decoding.
papers.key_findings:
MARCOS outperforms all continuous reasoning baselines and surpasses token-based CoT by 4.7% on GSM8K with up to 15.7x inference speedup.
The random variable R_k controls different aspects of reasoning, such as output length and format, without compromising accuracy.
MARCOS supports non-autoregressive decoding in the speaking stage, maintaining competitive accuracy.
Ablation studies show that deep thinking neurons, random variables, and sparsity loss are all critical components.
The model generalizes well to out-of-domain benchmarks like SVAMP and MultiArith.
papers.limitation:
Experiments primarily focus on mathematical reasoning tasks.
Evaluation is conducted on relatively basic mathematical problems rather than more challenging datasets like MATH or AIME.
The model is trained from scratch and lacks pretraining on massive corpora, limiting its broader capabilities.
future_direction: Develop a pretraining methodology for MARCOS on large, unstructured corpora.
Explore reinforcement learning algorithms that leverage step-level control over randomness for efficient exploration.
Integrate more advanced non-autoregressive decoding strategies to further accelerate inference.
papers.abstract: The current paradigm for reasoning in large language models (LLMs) involves models "thinking out loud" via a sequence of tokens, known as chain-of-thought (CoT). This approach, while effective, has several significant drawbacks. Firstly, inference requires autoregressive generation of often thousands of CoT tokens, which is slow and computationally expensive. Secondly, it constrains reasoning to the discrete space of tokens, creating an information bottleneck across reasoning steps. Thirdly, it fundamentally entangles reasoning with token generation, forcing LLMs to "think while speaking," which causes potentially short-sighted reasoning. In light of these limitations, we re-imagine reasoning in LLMs and present a new paradigm: MARCOS. In our approach, rather than autoregressively generating tokens, we model reasoning as a hidden Markov chain of continuous, high-dimensional "thoughts". Each reasoning step involves a transition of the internal thoughts, where explicit reasoning steps (which may consist of hundreds of tokens) serve as observable variables, which are windows to peek into the implicit thoughts. Since this latent process is incompatible with the standard supervised learning, we further propose a two-phase variational training scheme. Our experiments on three benchmarks demonstrate that MARCOS outperforms existing continuous reasoning methods and, for the first time, achieves performance comparable to token-based CoT, even surpassing it by 4.7% on GSM8K with up to 15.7x speedup in inference. Beyond this, MARCOS offers additional advantages, such as step-level instead of token-level control over randomness, opening significant opportunities for reinforcement learning and reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: A Implies B: Circuit Analysis in LLMs for Propositional Logical Reasoning
papers.research_question: How do large language models solve propositional logic problems? Are their reasoning mechanisms localized and modular, and what are the core components involved?
papers.core_contribution: The paper discovers that LLMs use sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, consisting of four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating, queried-rule moving, fact processing, and decision making. These circuits are similar across different models but show scale-dependent variations.
papers.conclusion: LLMs employ sparse, modular circuits for propositional logical reasoning, with specialized attention head families. These circuits are similar across models but exhibit scale-dependent differences, suggesting that mechanistic insights do not fully generalize across model sizes.
papers.key_findings:
All three models contain four families of attention heads with specialized roles: queried-rule locating heads, queried-rule mover heads, fact-processing heads, and decision heads.
The models perform lazy reasoning: the core circuit activates primarily after seeing the Question and the query variable.
The models reuse sub-circuits for different parts of the argument when possible.
Gemma-2-27B has additional logical-operator heads and a more parallel circuit compared to the more sequential Gemma-2-9B.
Small trained models (3-layer) perform intermingled reasoning, less modular than larger pre-trained models.
papers.limitation: Partial analysis of Gemma-2-27B due to computational constraints
future_direction: Fully validating the algorithm for LogOp chain reasoning in small transformers
papers.abstract: Due to the size and complexity of modern large language models (LLMs), it has proven challenging to uncover the underlying mechanisms that models use to solve reasoning problems. For instance, is their reasoning for a specific problem localized to certain parts of the network? Do they break down the reasoning problem into modular components that are then executed as sequential steps as we go deeper in the model? To better understand the reasoning capability of LLMs, we study a minimal propositional logic problem that requires combining multiple facts to arrive at a solution. By studying this problem on Mistral and Gemma models, up to 27B parameters, we illuminate the core components the models use to solve such logic problems. From a mechanistic interpretability point of view, we use causal mediation analysis to uncover the pathways and components of the LLMs' reasoning processes. Then, we offer fine-grained insights into the functions of attention heads in different layers. We not only find a sparse circuit that computes the answer, but we decompose it into sub-circuits that have four distinct and modular uses. Finally, we reveal that three distinct models -- Mistral-7B, Gemma-2-9B and Gemma-2-27B -- contain analogous but not identical mechanisms.

papers.title: Think-to-Talk or Talk-to-Think? When LLMs Come Up with an Answer in Multi-Hop Arithmetic Reasoning
papers.research_question: When during chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning do LLMs determine their final answer, and how causally dependent is the answer on the CoT explanation?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT generation, and the CoT explanations are faithful reflections of their internal computation, not post-hoc justifications.
papers.conclusion: LLMs compute answers iteratively during CoT, making CoT explanations faithful to the internal reasoning process.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs do not determine the final answer before CoT begins; instead, they compute sub-answers during CoT generation.
Linear probes show that answers become linearly separable in hidden states only after corresponding reasoning steps in CoT.
Causal interventions show that the final answer depends causally on the CoT part, especially the latter steps, showing recency bias.
The model's internal reasoning follows a recency bias: each step causally depends on the previous step.
For distractors (unnecessary variables), the model does not encode them in a linearly separable form, indicating efficient internal mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The study uses synthetic arithmetic tasks, which may not generalize to natural language reasoning.
The cause of incorrect answers in some instances remains unclear.
future_direction: Investigate more complex and natural language reasoning tasks.
Detailed analysis of error cases and internal representations of digits.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the incremental, internal problem-solving process of language models (LMs) with arithmetic multi-hop reasoning as a case study. We specifically investigate when LMs internally resolve sub/whole problems through first reading the problem statements, generating reasoning chains, and achieving the final answer to mechanistically interpret LMs' multi-hop problem-solving process. Our experiments reveal a systematic incremental reasoning strategy underlying LMs. They have not derived an answer at the moment they first read the problem; instead, they obtain (sub)answers while generating the reasoning chain. Therefore, the generated reasoning chains can be regarded as faithful reflections of the model's internal computation.

papers.title: Chain-of-Thought Tokens are Computer Program Variables
papers.research_question: What is the role of CoT tokens in LLMs for compositional reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: CoT tokens function like variables in computer programs, storing intermediate values that are used in subsequent computations and are causally related to the final output.
papers.conclusion: CoT tokens behave like variables in computer programs, storing intermediate values that are causally connected to the output, but models may learn shortcuts and there is a computational complexity limit.
papers.key_findings:
CoT is essential for solving compositional problems like multi-digit multiplication and dynamic programming.
Removing non-result tokens (keeping only intermediate results) does not harm performance, indicating that intermediate results are the key.
Intermediate results can be stored in different forms (e.g., latent tokens) without performance drop, unless compression exceeds a complexity limit.
Intervening on CoT token values changes subsequent reasoning and final output, showing causal relation.
Models sometimes take shortcuts in easy subproblems, making interventions fail.
papers.limitation:
No theoretical proof is provided for the hypothesis that CoT tokens function like variables.
Experiments are conducted on two synthetic tasks with one model (Qwen-2.5-1.5B), and not on real-world datasets.
future_direction: Generalization ability of CoT programs.
Identification of intermediate variable tokens in general tasks.
Estimation of computational complexity between variable tokens.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thoughts (CoT) requires large language models (LLMs) to generate intermediate steps before reaching the final answer, and has been proven effective to help LLMs solve complex reasoning tasks. However, the inner mechanism of CoT still remains largely unclear. In this paper, we empirically study the role of CoT tokens in LLMs on two compositional tasks: multi-digit multiplication and dynamic programming. While CoT is essential for solving these problems, we find that preserving only tokens that store intermediate results would achieve comparable performance. Furthermore, we observe that storing intermediate results in an alternative latent form will not affect model performance. We also randomly intervene some values in CoT, and notice that subsequent CoT tokens and the final answer would change correspondingly. These findings suggest that CoT tokens may function like variables in computer programs but with potential drawbacks like unintended shortcuts and computational complexity limits between tokens. The code and data are available at https://github.com/solitaryzero/CoTs_are_Variables.

papers.title: Failure Modes in Multi-Hop QA: The Weakest Link Law and the Recognition Bottleneck
papers.research_question: Does linear distance between supporting facts or their absolute position within the context govern multi-hop reasoning? Can MFAI effectively mitigate position bias in MHQA and isolate recognition errors from intrinsic synthesis limitations? Does extended test-time compute (System-2 reasoning) confer robustness against misleading attention cues?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'Weakest Link Effect' in multi-hop reasoning, where performance collapses to the level of the least visible evidence bucket, governed by absolute position. Introduces MFAI as a semantic probe to disentangle recognition failures from synthesis failures.
papers.conclusion: Multi-hop reasoning is constrained by the absolute position of the least visible evidence and driven primarily by a recognition bottleneck. Task topology modulates the impact of misleading attention cues, and thinking models can override position bias at a cost of increased compute.
papers.key_findings:
Multi-hop reasoning performance follows a 'Weakest Link Effect', collapsing to the level of the least visible evidence bucket, governed by absolute position rather than linear distance between facts.
Matched MFAI resolves recognition bottlenecks, improving accuracy in low-visibility positions, indicating failures are largely recognition-based rather than reasoning-based.
Unmatched (misleading) MFAI yields divergent effects modulated by task topology: entity-centric tasks with vertical reasoning chains are vulnerable, whereas event-centric tasks with horizontal evidence structures are more resilient.
Models utilizing extended test-time compute (System-2 reasoning) effectively locate and integrate required information, matching gold-only baselines even in noisy, long-context settings.
The 'Weakest Link Effect' and recognition bottleneck generalize across datasets (MuSiQue, NeoQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA), reasoning depths (2-, 3-, 4-hop), and model scales (7B–32B).
papers.limitation:
Core experiments cover two datasets (MuSiQue, NeoQA) and five models; supplementary evaluations extend to 2WikiMultiHopQA, 3-/4-hop subsets, and Qwen2.5-32B, but these use representative models rather than the full suite, and frontier-scale models (70B+) remain untested.
Did not perform a mechanistic analysis using logprobs or perplexity, nor explore prompt variations, different bucket...
future_direction: RAG reranking should prioritize high-visibility placement of critical evidence; training objectives should target recognition under noisy retrieval.
Developing lightweight mechanistic probes (e.g., attention patterns, logprob signals) would make position bias diagnosis practical.
Distilling self-verification from thinking models into standard inference remains open.
Whether other reasoning structures (e.g., comparative, temporal) exhibit distinct vulnerability profiles under the vertical–horizontal topology is an open question for task-specific mitigation.
papers.abstract: Despite scaling to massive context windows, Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle with multi-hop reasoning due to inherent position bias, which causes them to overlook information at certain positions. Whether these failures stem from an inability to locate evidence (recognition failure) or integrate it (synthesis failure) is unclear. We introduce Multi-Focus Attention Instruction (MFAI), a semantic probe to disentangle these mechanisms by explicitly steering attention towards selected positions. Across 5 LLMs on two multi-hop QA tasks (MuSiQue and NeoQA), we establish the "Weakest Link Law": multi-hop reasoning performance collapses to the performance level of the least visible evidence. Crucially, this failure is governed by absolute position rather than the linear distance between facts (performance variance $<3%$). We further identify a duality in attention steering: while matched MFAI resolves recognition bottlenecks, improving accuracy by up to 11.5% in low-visibility positions, misleading MFAI triggers confusion in real-world tasks but is successfully filtered in synthetic tasks. Finally, we demonstrate that "thinking" models that utilize System-2 reasoning, effectively locate and integrate the required information, matching gold-only baselines even in noisy, long-context settings.

papers.title: Expanding Computation Spaces of LLMs at Inference Time
papers.research_question: Whether language models can leverage artificially inserted sequences of filler tokens solely at inference time as expanded computation spaces, and how token types, numbers, insertion locations, training stage, and attention dynamics affect this.
papers.core_contribution: Language models can exploit filler tokens inserted at inference as expanded computation spaces to improve performance on QA and math tasks, with smaller models benefiting more, and attention analysis shows these spaces engage in meaningful computation.
papers.conclusion: Inserting filler tokens at inference provides expanded computation spaces that improve model performance, especially for smaller models, and these spaces are used meaningfully for answer inference as shown by attention analysis.
papers.key_findings:
Smaller models (e.g., 1.7B) benefit most from inserted filler tokens, with gains up to 12.372 percentage points, suggesting the spaces compensate for limited parameter capacity.
Optimal token types and counts vary across models; placing filler tokens directly before the final 'Answer:' token is most effective.
Models progressively learn to leverage these spaces during pretraining and instruction-tuning, as shown by checkpoint analysis.
Attention map analysis reveals filler tokens attend to questions and answer options, influencing answer selection, rather than being redundant.
Performance degrades sharply when too many tokens (e.g., >1024) are added, resembling the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon.
papers.limitation: Performance degrades when too many filler tokens are added, as models are not trained on such inputs.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) rationale enables language models to use additional task-related text for problem-solving, benefiting not only from detailed reasoning steps but also from the expanded computational space of longer inputs. Prior work has trained filler or special tokens to serve as additional computation spaces. In this study, we investigate whether language models can leverage artificially inserted sequences of filler tokens solely at inference. We first identify effective token types, numbers, and insertion locations, then examine at what stage of training models begin to exploit the expanded computation space, and finally analyze dynamics within these spaces via attention maps. Experiments on models ranging from 1.7B to 32B across open-domain QA and math tasks show that appropriate token types and counts vary, but placing filler tokens directly before the final 'Answer:' token is most effective. Smaller models benefit most, up to 12.372 percentage points in SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct, indicating that these spaces act as additional computational capacity rather than redundant input. Attention maps reveal that expanded spaces often continue the original attention mechanism and sometimes focus on questions or answer options, suggesting meaningful computation for problem-solving.

papers.title: Let's Think Dot by Dot: Hidden Computation in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent can transformers use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') to perform hidden computation and solve algorithmic tasks they cannot solve without intermediate tokens, and under what conditions does this occur?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can use meaningless filler tokens to solve hard algorithmic tasks they fail at without intermediate tokens, showing additional tokens provide computational benefits independent of token meaning, but learning to use filler tokens requires specific, dense supervision.
papers.conclusion: For certain parallelizable problems, transformers achieve improved performance with filler tokens instead of chain-of-thought tokens, meaning intermediate tokens can be used purely for computational capacity rather than faithful serial reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve perfect accuracy on 3SUM and high accuracy on 2SUM-Transform with filler tokens, while failing without them.
The performance gap between filler and no-filler settings increases with problem complexity (input length and dimension).
Filler token representations encode hidden, task-relevant computation, as shown by fine-tuning experiments.
Learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires training on parallelizable chain-of-thought data; instance-adaptive CoT data does not transfer.
Filler tokens extend transformer expressive power within the complexity class TC0, enabling solution of problems with deep quantifier nesting.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which token-parallelizable, TC0 algorithmic problems arise in natural language contexts.

Investigate whether natural-language text provides adequate supervision for filler-token computation, providing parallelizable supervision rather than non-parallelizable, instance-adaptive chains of thought.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought responses from language models improve performance across most benchmarks. However, it remains unclear to what extent these performance gains can be attributed to human-like task decomposition or simply the greater computation that additional tokens allow. We show that transformers can use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') in place of a chain of thought to solve two hard algorithmic tasks they could not solve when responding without intermediate tokens. However, we find empirically that learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires specific, dense supervision to converge. We also provide a theoretical characterization of the class of problems where filler tokens are useful in terms of the quantifier depth of a first-order formula. For problems satisfying this characterization, chain-of-thought tokens need not provide information about the intermediate computational steps involved in multi-token computations. In summary, our results show that additional tokens can provide computational benefits independent of token choice. The fact that intermediate tokens can act as filler tokens raises concerns about large language models engaging in unauditable, hidden computations that are increasingly detached from the observed chain-of-thought tokens.

papers.title: A Mechanistic Analysis of a Transformer Trained on a Symbolic Multi-Step Reasoning Task
papers.research_question: How does a transformer internally solve a symbolic multi-step reasoning task, specifically pathfinding in trees? What interpretable mechanisms does it use?
papers.core_contribution: The transformer implements an interpretable backward chaining algorithm for pathfinding, using deduction heads to climb the tree, parallel computation via register tokens, and a one-step lookahead heuristic.
papers.conclusion: The transformer demonstrates deductive reasoning up to a depth bounded by its layers, using parallelized backward chaining and heuristics, suggesting an inductive bias towards parallelized strategies for reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
The first layer attention head performs edge token concatenation, copying source node information to target node positions.
Deduction heads in subsequent layers implement backward chaining, climbing the tree one level per layer.
For paths longer than the number of layers, the model uses register tokens to perform parallel backward chaining and merges subpaths.
The model employs a one-step lookahead heuristic that identifies child nodes and increases logits for non-leaf children.
The model's reasoning depth is bounded by the number of layers, beyond which it resorts to heuristics.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is on a synthetic symbolic task, and it is unclear if similar mechanisms exist in large language models trained on natural language.
The analysis is limited to input where the edge list is presented in backward order; other arrangements may lead to different mechanisms.

papers.title: Visual Thoughts: A Unified Perspective of Understanding Multimodal Chain-of-Thought
papers.research_question: Is there a unified explanation for why different multimodal chain-of-thought paradigms enhance large vision-language models in distinct ways?
papers.core_contribution: The paper reveals that multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning improves large vision-language models by incorporating visual thoughts, which act as an intermediate cache for visual information, enabling more efficient and effective reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Visual thoughts provide a unified perspective for understanding how multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning enhances large vision-language models, acting as visual caches that improve information flow and reasoning performance.
papers.key_findings:
Removing visual thoughts from the reasoning process impairs model performance more than reasoning directly from the query alone.
Different expressions of visual thoughts (natural language, structured language, edited image, generative image) vary in effectiveness depending on task clarity and conciseness.
Visual thoughts serve as primary intermediaries, connecting input images to deeper transformer layers and facilitating advanced visual information processing.
Image-form visual thoughts consistently outperform text-form visual thoughts, especially in complex scenarios requiring detailed visual information.
Visual thoughts are more effective than simple image captions for conveying visual information in complex scenes, improving reasoning accuracy.
future_direction: Exploring the integration of multiple visual thoughts to enhance visual information transmission in multimodal chain-of-thought reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) have achieved significant success in multimodal tasks, with multimodal chain-of-thought (MCoT) further enhancing performance and interpretability. Recent MCoT methods fall into two categories: (i) Textual-MCoT (T-MCoT), which takes multimodal input and produces textual output; and (ii) Interleaved-MCoT (I-MCoT), which generates interleaved image-text outputs. Despite advances in both approaches, the mechanisms driving these improvements are not fully understood. To fill this gap, we first reveal that MCoT boosts LVLMs by incorporating visual thoughts, which convey image information to the reasoning process regardless of the MCoT format, depending only on clarity and conciseness of expression. Furthermore, to explore visual thoughts systematically, we define four distinct forms of visual thought expressions and analyze them comprehensively. Our findings demonstrate that these forms differ in clarity and conciseness, yielding varying levels of MCoT improvement. Additionally, we explore the internal nature of visual thoughts, finding that visual thoughts serve as intermediaries between the input image and reasoning to deeper transformer layers, enabling more advanced visual information transmission. We hope that the visual thoughts can inspire further breakthroughs for future MCoT research.

papers.title: Reasoning Beyond Words ? Exploring framework for hidden state reasoning
papers.research_question: Can reasoning in a continuous latent space, as opposed to the language space, lead to more efficient and effective reasoning in LLMs, particularly for tasks requiring planning and search?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Coconut, a method for reasoning in a continuous latent space by feeding the last hidden state back as the next input embedding, which enables emergent tree search behavior and improves reasoning efficiency and accuracy on certain tasks.
papers.conclusion: Reasoning in latent space leads to advanced emergent behaviors like BFS, and Coconut enhances LLM performance across reasoning tasks, with potential for future scaling and research.
papers.key_findings:
Coconut outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require planning and search (ProsQA).
Continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, enabling a breadth-first search (BFS) pattern.
Coconut provides a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency (fewer tokens) compared to CoT.
The multi-stage training curriculum is crucial for learning latent reasoning; without it, performance drops.
Increasing the number of continuous thoughts per reasoning step (c) can improve performance up to a point.
papers.limitation:
Training requires a multi-stage curriculum; without it, performance drops significantly.
Larger models (Llama) show less pronounced gains, possibly due to extensive language-focused pre-training.
Training efficiency is challenging due to sequential forward passes, limiting parallelism.
future_direction: Refine and scale latent reasoning to pretraining for better generalization.
Combine iCoT and Coconut for improved training.
Develop better strategies for learning reasoning in latent space without supervision from language reasoning chains.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are typically constrained to reason in the language space, where they express the reasoning process through a chain-of-thought (CoT) to solve complex problems. However, the language space may not always be optimal for reasoning. Most word tokens primarily ensure textual coherence and are not essential for reasoning, while some critical tokens require complex planning and pose challenges to LLMs. To explore the potential of reasoning beyond language, we introduce a new paradigm called Coconut (Chain of Continuous Thought). Coconut utilizes the last hidden state of the LLM as a representation of the reasoning state, termed "continuous thought." Instead of decoding this state into words, we feed it back to the model as the next input embedding directly in the continuous space. This latent reasoning paradigm enables an advanced reasoning pattern, where continuous thoughts can encode multiple alternative next steps, allowing the model to perform a breadth-first search (BFS) rather than committing prematurely to a single deterministic path as in CoT. Coconut outperforms CoT on logical reasoning tasks that require substantial search during planning and achieves a better trade-off between accuracy and efficiency.

papers.title: Fine-Tuning is Subgraph Search: A New Lens on Learning Dynamics
papers.research_question: This paper investigates how fine-tuning works from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, viewing fine-tuning as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within the model's computational graph.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit-tuning, a fine-tuning method that dynamically localizes and optimizes subgraphs (circuits) within a model's computational graph, enabling analysis of learning dynamics and balancing task performance with general capabilities.
papers.conclusion: Circuit-tuning provides a new method for studying learning dynamics from a mechanistic interpretability perspective, offering insights into how fine-tuning works and enabling more precise fine-tuning that balances task performance and general capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit-tuning provides better training stability and preserves language modeling ability better than full fine-tuning.
The functionality of specific attention heads (Subject Attribute Heads) can reverse during fine-tuning to adapt to new tasks.
Some attention heads (Subject Identification Heads) preserve their functions and are shared before and after fine-tuning.
Nodes within a circuit cooperate through division of labor and indirect interactions to complete tasks.
Edges in the computational graph exhibit strengthening and weakening akin to Hebbian learning during fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: The study of mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer a model to explain its behaviors. While recent studies have focused on the static mechanism of a certain behavior, the learning dynamics inside a model remain to be explored. In this work, we develop a fine-tuning method for analyzing the mechanism behind learning. Inspired by the concept of intrinsic dimension, we view a model as a computational graph with redundancy for a specific task, and treat the fine-tuning process as a search for and optimization of a subgraph within this graph. Based on this hypothesis, we propose circuit-tuning, an algorithm that iteratively builds the subgraph for a specific task and updates the relevant parameters in a heuristic way. We first validate our hypothesis through a carefully designed experiment and provide a detailed analysis of the learning dynamics during fine-tuning. Subsequently, we conduct experiments on more complex tasks, demonstrating that circuit-tuning could strike a balance between the performance on the target task and the general capabilities. Our work offers a new analytical method for the dynamics of fine-tuning, provides new findings on the mechanisms behind the training process, and inspires the design of superior algorithms for the training of neural networks.

papers.title: Emergence of Superposition: Unveiling the Training Dynamics of Chain of Continuous Thought
papers.research_question: How does the superposition mechanism in chain of continuous thought emerge during gradient-based training?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that gradient-based training of continuous CoT leads to bounded attention logits (index-matching logit), which enables superposition and balances exploration and exploitation in reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Gradient-based training naturally leads to superposition in continuous CoT, with bounded attention logits playing a key role in balancing exploration and exploitation during reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Under COCONUT training, the index-matching logit remains bounded, unlike in discrete settings where it diverges.
Bounded logits allow the model to maintain a superposition of multiple plausible reasoning traces.
The bounded logit balances exploration and exploitation: it exploits local graph structure while exploring multiple paths.
In the thought generation stage, the model performs one-step expansion, aggregating reachable nodes into the continuous thought.
In the prediction stage, the model learns to combine residual carryover and candidate lift signals to correctly predict the reachable node.
papers.limitation: Theoretical analysis is limited to a simplified two-layer transformer with orthonormal embeddings.
future_direction: Extending the theoretical analysis to deeper transformers and more complex tasks.
Comprehensive study of hyperparameter interactions in training.
papers.abstract: Previous work shows that the chain of continuous thought (continuous CoT) improves the reasoning capability of large language models (LLMs) by enabling implicit parallel thinking, and a subsequent work provided theoretical insight by showing that a two-layer transformer equipped with continuous CoT can efficiently solve directed graph reachability by maintaining a superposition of multiple reasoning traces in the continuous thought. However, it remains unclear how the superposition mechanism is naturally learned from gradient-based training methods. To fill this gap, we theoretically analyze the training dynamics of a simplified two-layer transformer on the directed graph reachability problem to unveil how the superposition mechanism emerges during training in two training stages -- (i) a thought-generation stage that autoregressively expands the continuous thought, and (ii) a prediction stage that converts the thought into the final answer. Our analysis reveals that during training using continuous thought, the index-matching logit, an important quantity which reflects the strength of the model's local search ability, will first increase and then remain bounded under mild assumptions. The bounded index-matching logit effectively balances exploration and exploitation during the reasoning process: the model will exploit local problem structures to identify plausible search traces, and assign comparable weights to multiple such traces to explore when it is uncertain about which solution is correct, which results in superposition. Our experimental results tracking the growth of logits further validate our theory.

papers.title: Beyond the Last Answer: Your Reasoning Trace Uncovers More than You Think
papers.research_question: Does the final answer reliably represent the model’s optimal conclusion, and can alternative reasoning paths yield different results?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a method to analyze intermediate reasoning steps (subthoughts) in LLM reasoning traces, showing that aggregating answers from subthought completions (mode) improves accuracy and that answer consistency (entropy) correlates with correctness.
papers.conclusion: Evaluating LLMs based solely on the final answer of a reasoning trace can be suboptimal. Analyzing intermediate subthoughts and aggregating answers via mode improves accuracy and provides a signal for reliability.
papers.key_findings:
Selecting the most frequent answer (mode) from completions originating at intermediate subthoughts significantly boosts accuracy compared to relying solely on the final answer of the initial trace.
The distribution of answers generated from subthoughts provides a valuable signal: high consistency (low entropy) correlates with correct baseline solutions, while high fluctuation (high entropy) is characteristic of incorrect solutions.
Non-greedy sampling for subthought completions often yields larger accuracy improvements compared to greedy sampling.
future_direction: Future work could explore integrating these consistency signals into decoding or training.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) leverage step-by-step reasoning to solve complex problems. Standard evaluation practice involves generating a complete reasoning trace and assessing the correctness of the final answer presented at its conclusion. In this paper, we challenge the reliance on the final answer by posing the following two questions: Does the final answer reliably represent the model's optimal conclusion? Can alternative reasoning paths yield different results? To answer these questions, we analyze intermediate reasoning steps, termed subthoughts, and propose a method based on our findings. Our approach involves segmenting a reasoning trace into sequential subthoughts based on linguistic cues. We start by prompting the model to generate continuations from the end-point of each intermediate subthought. We extract a potential answer from every completed continuation originating from different subthoughts. We find that aggregating these answers by selecting the most frequent one (the mode) often yields significantly higher accuracy compared to relying solely on the answer derived from the original complete trace. Analyzing the consistency among the answers derived from different subthoughts reveals characteristics that correlate with the model's confidence and correctness, suggesting potential for identifying less reliable answers. Our experiments across various LLMs and challenging mathematical reasoning datasets (AIME2024 and AIME2025) show consistent accuracy improvements, with gains reaching up to 13\% and 10\% respectively. Implementation is available at: https://github.com/hammoudhasan/SubthoughtReasoner.

papers.title: Diagnosing Pathological Chain-of-Thought in Reasoning Models
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is fundamental to modern LLM architectures and represents a critical intervention point for AI safety. However, CoT reasoning may exhibit failure modes that we note as pathologies, which prevent it from being useful for monitoring. Prior work has identified three distinct pathologies: post-hoc rationalization, where models generate plausible explanations backwards from predetermined answers; encoded reasoning, where intermediate steps conceal information within seemingly interpretable text; and internalized reasoning, where models replace explicit reasoning with meaningless filler tokens while computing internally. To better understand and discriminate between these pathologies, we create a set of concrete metrics that are simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, and task-agnostic. To validate our approach, we develop model organisms deliberately trained to exhibit specific CoT pathologies. Our work provides a practical toolkit for assessing CoT pathologies, with direct implications for training-time monitoring.

papers.title: exBERT: A Visual Analysis Tool to Explore Learned Representations in Transformer Models
papers.research_question: How can we develop an interactive tool to explore learned representations and attentions in Transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces EXBERT, an interactive visualization tool for exploring learned representations and attentions in Transformer models, enabling hypothesis formulation and replication of prior analyses.
papers.conclusion: EXBERT is a tool that provides interactive insights into Transformer models' representations and attentions, facilitating hypothesis generation and analysis.
papers.key_findings:
EXBERT can replicate prior findings on BERT's attention heads learning linguistic dependencies such as AUX and POBJ.
BERT's embeddings encode linguistic information progressively across layers, with verbs becoming more prominent in later layers.
EXBERT detects gender bias in GPT-2 by showing that it predicts gendered pronouns based on stereotypical associations.
GPT-2's attention heads learn syntactic structures like AUX and DOBJ dependencies, similar to BERT.
The tool allows for interactive exploration and quick hypothesis testing of model behavior through attention visualization and corpus similarity search.
papers.limitation: EXBERT only presents statistics across a small number of neighbors for a single token at a time, which may not reveal global model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large Transformer-based language models can route and reshape complex information via their multi-headed attention mechanism. Although the attention never receives explicit supervision, it can exhibit recognizable patterns following linguistic or positional information. Analyzing the learned representations and attentions is paramount to furthering our understanding of the inner workings of these models. However, analyses have to catch up with the rapid release of new models and the growing diversity of investigation techniques. To support analysis for a wide variety of models, we introduce EXBERT, a tool to help humans conduct flexible, interactive investigations and formulate hypotheses for the model-internal reasoning process. EXBERT provides insights into the meaning of the contextual representations and attention by matching a humanspecified input to similar contexts in large annotated datasets. By aggregating the annotations of the matched contexts, EXBERT can quickly replicate findings from literature and extend them to previously not analyzed models.

papers.title: Unveiling and Causalizing CoT: A Causal Pespective
papers.research_question: How can Chain-of-Thought reasoning be made both correct and understandable by modeling causality?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a causal perspective to unveil the mechanism of Chain-of-Thought reasoning and proposes CauCoT, a method to causalize CoT steps, ensuring correctness and understandability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that causality is crucial for CoT reasoning, and CauCoT provides an effective method to causalize CoT, improving LLMs' reasoning ability.
papers.key_findings:
CauCoT significantly improves reasoning accuracy over baseline methods like standard CoT and PB on multiple datasets.
The causality between reasoning steps, measured by CACE and FSCE, is strongly correlated with reasoning performance.
CauCoT effectively corrects common causal errors such as causality measure error, collider error, causal sensitivity error, and mediation error.
Hyperparameter experiments show that balancing logic and answer aspects in causal effect measurement is important for optimal performance.
Ablation studies confirm the necessity of components like first-step causal effect validation and refinement processes.
papers.abstract: Although Chain-of-Thought (CoT) has achieved remarkable success in enhancing the reasoning ability of large language models (LLMs), the mechanism of CoT remains a ``black box''. Even if the correct answers can frequently be obtained, existing CoTs struggle to make the reasoning understandable to human. In this paper, we unveil and causalize CoT from a causal perspective to ensure both correctness and understandability of all reasoning steps (to the best of our knowledge, the first such). We model causality of CoT via structural causal models (SCM) to unveil the reasoning mechanism of CoT. To measure the causality of CoT, we define the CoT Average Causal Effect (CACE) to test the causal relations between steps. For those steps without causality (wrong or unintelligible steps), we design a role-playing causal query algorithm to causalize these steps, resulting a causalized CoT with all steps correct and understandable. Experimental results on both open-source and closed-source LLMs demonstrate that the causal errors commonly in steps are effectively corrected and the reasoning ability of LLMs is significantly improved.

papers.title: Circular Reasoning: Understanding Self-Reinforcing Loops in Large Reasoning Models
papers.research_question: What is the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, and how can we systematically analyze its mechanisms and predict its onset?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies the 'Circular Reasoning' failure mode in Large Reasoning Models, introduces LoopBench for systematic evaluation, analyzes the mechanisms (state collapse, triggers, persistence via V-shaped attention), and proposes an early prediction method using CUSUM on hidden states.
papers.conclusion: Circular reasoning is a critical failure mode in LRMs that stems from intrinsic generation mechanisms, and the proposed analysis and prediction method provide a foundation for improving reasoning stability.
papers.key_findings:
Circular reasoning manifests as two distinct loop types: numerical loops (universal) and statement loops (prevalent in reasoning models).
LoopBench triggers significantly higher repetition rates than existing benchmarks, revealing model fragility.
The loop onset is triggered by reasoning impasses and sustained by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention pattern.
Early prediction of statement loops is feasible by monitoring hidden state shifts with the CUSUM algorithm.
Decoding strategies mitigate but do not eliminate repetition, indicating an inherent trade-off between loop and accuracy.
papers.limitation:
LoopBench focuses on specific task patterns (high-precision arithmetic and complex recursive reasoning) and may not cover all reasoning scenarios.
The early prediction method is only validated for statement loops, not numerical loops.
The analysis is primarily conducted on open-source models, limiting generalizability to closed-source models.
future_direction: Expand LoopBench to more diverse tasks and domains.
Investigate loop mitigation strategies, such as dynamic decoding or architectural modifications.
Extend the analysis to more model architectures and scales.
papers.abstract: Despite the success of test-time scaling, Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) frequently encounter repetitive loops that lead to computational waste and inference failure. In this paper, we identify a distinct failure mode termed Circular Reasoning. Unlike traditional model degeneration, this phenomenon manifests as a self-reinforcing trap where generated content acts as a logical premise for its own recurrence, compelling the reiteration of preceding text. To systematically analyze this phenomenon, we introduce LoopBench, a dataset designed to capture two distinct loop typologies: numerical loops and statement loops. Mechanistically, we characterize circular reasoning as a state collapse exhibiting distinct boundaries, where semantic repetition precedes textual repetition. We reveal that reasoning impasses trigger the loop onset, which subsequently persists as an inescapable cycle driven by a self-reinforcing V-shaped attention mechanism. Guided by these findings, we employ the Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) algorithm to capture these precursors for early loop prediction. Experiments across diverse LRMs validate its accuracy and elucidate the stability of long-chain reasoning.

papers.title: Building Interpretable Models for Moral Decision-Making
papers.research_question: How do neural networks make moral decisions on trolley-style dilemmas, and where do moral biases originate within their architectures?
papers.core_contribution: Designs a 2-layer transformer optimized for moral reasoning tasks, achieving 77% accuracy on Moral Machine data, and combines interpretability methods to map internal mechanisms of moral judgment.
papers.conclusion: Demonstrates that small, custom transformers can achieve moral competence and be transparently analyzed, enabling targeted interventions for bias mitigation.
papers.key_findings:
The model learns a moral hierarchy where characters like Pregnant and Stroller have positive causal effects, while Criminal has negative effects.
Moral biases localize to distinct computational stages: legality bias in Layer 0 and species bias in Layer 1.
Circuit probing identifies sparse subnetworks in the MLP block that causally implement moral scoring.
The model shows functional specialization with different attention heads specializing in different bias dimensions.
Small, custom transformers can achieve moral competence while remaining interpretable, enabling targeted bias interventions.
papers.limitation: Training on aggregate human preferences inherits cultural biases.
future_direction: Extend the approach to traditional large language models on moral questions.
papers.abstract: We build a custom transformer model to study how neural networks make moral decisions on trolley-style dilemmas. The model processes structured scenarios using embeddings that encode who is affected, how many people, and which outcome they belong to. Our 2-layer architecture achieves 77% accuracy on Moral Machine data while remaining small enough for detailed analysis. We use different interpretability techniques to uncover how moral reasoning distributes across the network, demonstrating that biases localize to distinct computational stages among other findings.

papers.title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: A Theoretical Perspective
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms behind Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and how does it unlock the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) for mathematical and reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper theoretically proves that bounded-depth Transformers without Chain-of-Thought (CoT) require super-polynomial size to solve basic mathematical tasks, while constant-size autoregressive Transformers with CoT can solve them, and extends this to show CoT enables solving dynamic programming problems.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought is the key to unlocking the reasoning capabilities of autoregressive Transformers, both theoretically and empirically, by allowing step-by-step generation that overcomes the expressivity limitations of bounded-depth models.
papers.key_findings:
Bounded-depth log-precision Transformers of polynomial size cannot directly solve arithmetic and linear equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with input length.
Autoregressive Transformers of constant depth and size can generate correct CoT solutions for arithmetic and linear equation tasks.
LLMs with CoT can solve a general class of decision-making problems formulated as dynamic programming.
Experimental results show Transformers fail to directly predict answers but consistently learn to generate correct step-by-step CoT solutions given sufficient demonstrations.
CoT increases the effective depth of the Transformer circuit, allowing it to solve problems beyond the TC0 complexity class.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have discovered that Chain-of-Thought prompting (CoT) can dramatically improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when dealing with complex tasks involving mathematics or reasoning. Despite the enormous empirical success, the underlying mechanisms behind CoT and how it unlocks the potential of LLMs remain elusive. In this paper, we take a first step towards theoretically answering these questions. Specifically, we examine the expressivity of LLMs with CoT in solving fundamental mathematical and decision-making problems. By using circuit complexity theory, we first give impossibility results showing that bounded-depth Transformers are unable to directly produce correct answers for basic arithmetic/equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with respect to the input length. In contrast, we then prove by construction that autoregressive Transformers of constant size suffice to solve both tasks by generating CoT derivations using a commonly used math language format. Moreover, we show LLMs with CoT can handle a general class of decision-making problems known as Dynamic Programming, thus justifying its power in tackling complex real-world tasks. Finally, an extensive set of experiments show that, while Transformers always fail to directly predict the answers, they can consistently learn to generate correct solutions step-by-step given sufficient CoT demonstrations.

papers.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
papers.research_question: Do circuit analyses of LLMs generalize across training time and model scale?
papers.core_contribution: Circuit analyses are consistent across training and scale: task abilities and supporting functional components emerge at similar token counts across model sizes, and the overarching algorithms implemented by circuits remain stable even when individual components change.
papers.conclusion: Circuit analyses generalize well over both training and scale, suggesting that studies on small models at the end of pre-training can inform understanding of larger models and models with longer training.
papers.key_findings:
Task abilities and functional components (e.g., induction heads, name-mover heads) emerge consistently at similar token counts across different model scales.
The algorithm implemented by a circuit remains stable over training even when the specific attention heads implementing it change.
Circuit size correlates with model size and can fluctuate over time while the algorithm remains the same.
Components like induction heads emerge around 2B tokens across scales, paralleling task learning curves.
Circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training provide insights that generalize to larger models and longer training runs.
papers.limitation:
The study does not include fine-tuning or other post-training techniques.
Circuit completeness is challenging to verify.
The findings need validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
future_direction: Validation on more complex circuits and those based on SAE latents.
Investigating the load-balancing mechanism that maintains task performance when components change.
papers.abstract: Most currently deployed large language models (LLMs) undergo continuous training or additional finetuning. By contrast, most research into LLMs' internal mechanisms focuses on models at one snapshot in time (the end of pre-training), raising the question of whether their results generalize to real-world settings. Existing studies of mechanisms over time focus on encoder-only or toy models, which differ significantly from most deployed models. In this study, we track how model mechanisms, operationalized as circuits, emerge and evolve across 300 billion tokens of training in decoder-only LLMs, in models ranging from 70 million to 2.8 billion parameters. We find that task abilities and the functional components that support them emerge consistently at similar token counts across scale. Moreover, although such components may be implemented by different attention heads over time, the overarching algorithm that they implement remains. Surprisingly, both these algorithms and the types of components involved therein can replicate across model scale. These results suggest that circuit analyses conducted on small models at the end of pre-training can provide insights that still apply after additional pre-training and over model scale.

papers.title: Trust Me, I'm an Expert: Decoding and Steering Authority Bias in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Investigates whether language models exhibit systematic bias based on the perceived expertise of endorsement sources, and how source expertise influences model behavior across domains.
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that LLMs exhibit hierarchical authority bias, becoming more susceptible to incorrect endorsements from higher-expertise sources, and shows that this bias can be reduced by steering the model's residual stream.
papers.conclusion: LLMs prioritize source credibility over semantic correctness, making them vulnerable to authority bias, but this bias can be mechanistically isolated and controlled via steering vectors.
papers.key_findings:
Models show progressively larger accuracy gains with correct endorsements as source expertise increases.
High-expertise incorrect endorsements induce confident errors, with models becoming more confident in wrong answers.
Reasoning models remain susceptible to expert endorsement despite chain-of-thought capabilities.
Mathematical reasoning tasks show lower robustness rates (largest susceptibility), while medical tasks show higher resistance.
Authority bias can be mechanistically reduced by subtracting a steering vector extracted from the residual stream.
papers.limitation:
Experiments are constrained to smaller open-source models (up to 32B parameters); frontier-scale models may exhibit different patterns of authority susceptibility.
Evaluation only covers four domains (mathematical, legal, and medical reasoning); broader domain coverage would strengthen generalization claims.
Endorsement format is limited to single, explicit answer statements without variations in phrasing, confidence levels, or reasoning justification.
Have not yet conducted comprehensive analysis across layers or utilized interpretability methods like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) to fully characterize the underlying representations.
future_direction: larger-scale evaluations
richer interaction scenarios
deeper mechanistic investigations
papers.abstract: Prior research demonstrates that performance of language models on reasoning tasks can be influenced by suggestions, hints and endorsements. However, the influence of endorsement source credibility remains underexplored. We investigate whether language models exhibit systematic bias based on the perceived expertise of the provider of the endorsement. Across 4 datasets spanning mathematical, legal, and medical reasoning, we evaluate 11 models using personas representing four expertise levels per domain. Our results reveal that models are increasingly susceptible to incorrect/misleading endorsements as source expertise increases, with higher-authority sources inducing not only accuracy degradation but also increased confidence in wrong answers. We also show that this authority bias is mechanistically encoded within the model and a model can be steered away from the bias, thereby improving its performance even when an expert gives a misleading endorsement.

papers.title: When Can Large Reasoning Models Save Thinking? Mechanistic Analysis of Behavioral Divergence in Reasoning
papers.abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) have significantly advanced performance on complex tasks, yet their tendency to overthink introduces inefficiencies. This study investigates the internal mechanisms of reinforcement learning (RL)-trained LRMs when prompted to save thinking, revealing three distinct thinking modes: no thinking (NT), explicit thinking (ET), and implicit thinking (IT).
